title: Draupadi's question
hook: Draupadi asks the elders to their faces, and Bhishma answers: the ways of dharma are subtle
carry: the ways of dharma are subtle

segments.voice: Yesterday a messenger carried Draupadi's question back and forth: which had Yudhishthira lost first, himself or her? And he said nothing.

This part of the story is hard, and i'll tell it plainly and with care. Duhshasana goes to the women's rooms. Draupadi tries to get away, and he seizes her by the hair and drags her into the assembly. The telling says she's in a single garment, and in distress. Here's what stands out about her, in a hall full of men who have just watched her gambled away. She doesn't only cry out. She argues.
screen: `A HARD SCENE, TOLD WITH CARE.` → `DRAGGED INTO THE HALL.` → `SHE ARGUES.`

segments.voice: She looks at the elders and asks how they can sit and watch this. Where has the dharma of these kings gone, she asks, if they can see this done and stay silent? Then, plainly: was I won, or not? Answer it. Bhishma answers. What he says is honest in its way, and painful. The ways of dharma are subtle, he says. One who owns nothing can't stake what belongs to another. And yet a wife, as the custom of the time held, is under her husband's authority. Holding both, he says he can't settle it. He adds that Yudhishthira himself admits he was beaten, and that Shakuni is a master at dice. The question has gone up to the eldest, and the eldest has set it down again, unsettled. Draupadi answers him sharply. Yudhishthira was called to the game, she says, by players skilled and crooked, and he had no skill at it himself. How can anyone say he played by free choice? Some readers hear Bhishma's answer as cowardice. Others hear an old man caught between two rules, refusing to pretend the knot is simple. The poem doesn't decide that for us. What it does show is this: when the person with the most authority in the room says it's subtle, the person who pays for that subtlety is still standing in the middle of the hall, waiting.
screen: `WHERE IS THE DHARMA OF THESE KINGS?` · `BHISHMA: THE WAYS OF DHARMA ARE SUBTLE.` · `TWO RULES, AND NO VERDICT.` · `HE DIDN'T CHOOSE TO PLAY.` · then, large: `SHE IS STILL WAITING.`

segments.voice: Recall a time you asked for a clear answer and heard: it's complicated. Maybe it was; maybe it was also a way of not answering. Hold both possibilities, the way Bhishma held his two rules, and breathe slowly with a question that isn't settled; if you pray, bring it into your prayer, and if not, simply let it rest.
Draupadi's question. Asked to the elders' faces, and answered by Bhishma: the ways of dharma are subtle, and he can't settle it.
Your line: the ways of dharma are subtle. Subtle, and still someone is waiting for an answer. Go gently.

howItsDone: Bhishma's reply that dharma is subtle is quoted and debated by Hindu teachers and readers as a picture of how hard right action can be, and of what silence costs.

chat.says: When Draupadi asked the elders if she'd been won, what did Bhishma say?
options: That the ways of dharma are subtle; he weighed two rules and couldn't settle it.
That he would answer her only once Krishna had arrived in the hall.
That Yudhishthira had never really staked her in the first place.
chat.meaning: Bhishma said the ways of dharma are subtle: one who owns nothing can't stake another, yet a wife was under her husband's authority.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (Duhshasana brings Draupadi into the assembly; her appeal to the elders; Bhishma's answer that morality is subtle; Draupadi's reply that Yudhishthira was made to play by skilled and deceitful players)

notes: Content care: Draupadi seized by the hair and dragged into the hall in a single garment; told without further detail. Confirm tone.

All paraphrase. Confirm Bhishma's two rules (one without wealth cannot stake another's; wives are under their husbands' control) and his statement that he cannot decide; confirm he cites Yudhishthira's own admission of defeat and Shakuni's skill.
Confirm Draupadi's reply: Yudhishthira, unskilled, was summoned and made to play by skilled, wicked, deceitful players; how can he be said to have played of his own will.
'As the custom of the time held' frames Bhishma's second rule as his citation of custom, not the script's view; a Keeper may prefer different wording.
